opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few big ones, and honestly they're what make the area exciting right now.

The first is really about understanding why and when diffusion works for discrete data. For continuous data like images, we have a pretty mature theory: score matching, the connection to stochastic differential equations, all of that. For text, the tokens are discrete, so we've had to come up with different formulations, like masked diffusion or approaches based on learning ratios of the data distribution, what we called concrete scores. These work surprisingly well in practice, but our understanding of what the right noising process is, and what the right parameterization is, is still pretty incomplete. Is masking the best corruption process? Are there better ones that let the model revise tokens it already committed to? I don't think we know yet.

The second is scaling. Autoregressive models have had years of very careful work on scaling laws, architectures, training recipes, and data. With diffusion language models, we're only beginning to see what happens at large scale. There's some evidence they may be more data-efficient, since they effectively see each sequence under many different corruption patterns, which acts a bit like built-in augmentation. But whether they match or beat autoregressive models per unit of compute across the board is an open empirical and theoretical question.

Third is inference, which is the main practical selling point. The appeal is that you generate many tokens in parallel and refine them, so you can be much faster than token-by-token decoding. But there's a real tension between parallelism and quality. When you unmask many tokens at once, you're implicitly assuming they're conditionally independent, which they aren't. So how do you design samplers, schedules, and distillation methods that get you most of the speed without degrading coherence? That's both a theoretical and an engineering question.

Then there's everything around alignment and post-training. The whole RLHF and reasoning toolkit was built around models with tractable left-to-right likelihoods. With diffusion models, the likelihood is usually only available as a bound, so adapting reinforcement learning, preference optimization, and things like chain-of-thought reasoning isn't straightforward. There's also an interesting question of whether diffusion enables new kinds of reasoning. The model can look at the whole output at once and revise it globally, which might suit planning, code, or constrained generation better than strictly sequential generation.

Finally, there's controllability. In images, guidance techniques gave us a lot of control over generation. Bringing that same flexibility to text, like infilling, editing, or satisfying constraints anywhere in the sequence, is a natural strength of the diffusion framework, but we're still figuring out how to do it well.

So overall I'd say the field is roughly where image diffusion was a few years ago. We've shown it can work and be competitive, and now there's a lot of fundamental science to do to understand it and push it further.

r001.rationale: It identifies the right noising or corruption process for discrete text as an unresolved question.

r002.rationale: It discusses training and inference separately but does not explain that the inference procedure can be decoupled from the training procedure.

r003.rationale: It does not mention adapting numerical differential-equation solvers to speed sampling in continuous diffusion models.

r004.rationale: It mentions guidance and controllability, but does not identify how to incorporate information throughout the diffusion process as an open question.

r005.rationale: It says continuous image diffusion is more mature than text diffusion, but does not mention video diffusion models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few big ones, and they're actually pretty fundamental.

The first is really about scaling and the scaling laws. We have a very good understanding at this point of how autoregressive models behave as you scale up data and compute. For diffusion language models we're still in the early days. We've seen encouraging signs, both from our own work at Inception with Mercury and from what other groups have published, that these models scale in a similar way, but we don't yet have the same kind of precise, well-established picture. Are there regimes where diffusion is more data-efficient, or more compute-efficient? That's a very open empirical question.

The second is about the training objective itself. Autoregressive models have this very clean story: you maximize likelihood, next-token prediction, and that's it. With discrete diffusion, there are a lot of design choices. How do you corrupt the data? Masking, uniform noise, something else? What's the right noise schedule? How do you weight the different noise levels in the loss? Each of those choices changes what the model learns and how well it generates, and we don't have a principled theory that tells us which one is optimal for language. There's also a gap between the training objective and the way we actually sample, and closing that gap is a big research direction.

Third, and this is the one I personally find most interesting, is what new capabilities you unlock by not being constrained to generate left to right. Diffusion models can refine their outputs. They can revisit earlier tokens, they can do infilling natively, they can in principle plan more globally over the sequence. So the question is: does that translate into better reasoning, better controllability, better error correction? Or does it mostly just buy you speed? I believe it's more than speed, but demonstrating that rigorously is still open.

Then there's the question of how to do the things we already know how to do for autoregressive models. Alignment, RLHF, chain-of-thought style reasoning, long context. A lot of the techniques that make modern LLMs useful were developed with the autoregressive factorization in mind. For example, if you want to do reinforcement learning, you need likelihoods or some surrogate for them, and in diffusion models the likelihood is only available as a bound. So figuring out the right way to do post-training in this paradigm is a very active area.

And finally there's the inference side. The whole appeal of parallel generation is that you can produce many tokens at once, but there's a tradeoff between the number of denoising steps and quality. Understanding that tradeoff, and developing better samplers, better ways to decide which tokens to commit to and when, is both a scientific question and a very practical one.

So I'd summarize it as: scaling, objectives, new capabilities, post-training, and inference. Each of those has a lot of room, and that's what makes it an exciting time to work on this.

r001.rationale: It identifies unresolved training choices, including how to corrupt data (masking, uniform noise, or another method) and the noise schedule.

r002.rationale: It describes a gap between the training objective and the way models are sampled, and says closing that gap is an active research direction.

r003.rationale: It does not mention numerical differential-equation solvers or their use to accelerate sampling in continuous diffusion models.

r004.rationale: It discusses weighting noise levels in the training loss and deciding when to commit tokens, but does not clearly identify how best to incorporate information throughout the diffusion process as an open question.

r005.rationale: It calls diffusion language models early in development compared with autoregressive models, but does not compare them with continuous image or video diffusion research.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest questions is what the right diffusion process is for language. With images, there’s a very natural notion of adding a little bit of noise and gradually destroying the signal. For text, which is discrete, that choice is much less obvious. You can mask tokens, you can replace tokens, you can move into a continuous representation. But what makes one of those choices fundamentally better than another?

Another question is how to exploit parallel generation effectively. In principle, you can update many tokens at once, rather than generate everything from left to right. But those updates have to be coordinated. So how many rounds of refinement do you actually need to produce something coherent? And how does that tradeoff change as you scale the model or increase the length of the sequence?

Then there’s the question of what these models are especially good at. Being able to revise an earlier decision seems very useful for satisfying constraints or filling in different parts of a document. But does that translate into better reasoning, or do we need different training objectives to get that benefit? I think understanding that connection between the generation process and the capabilities we want is a really interesting open direction.

r001.rationale: It identifies choosing the right diffusion process for language as a major open question and compares possible choices such as masking, replacement, and continuous representations.

r002.rationale: It does not explain how inference and training procedures are decoupled.

r003.rationale: It does not mention numerical differential-equation solvers or their use to accelerate sampling.

r004.rationale: It asks which diffusion process to use, but does not identify how to incorporate information throughout that process as an open question.

r005.rationale: It says the diffusion-process choice is less obvious for discrete text than for images, but does not state that research on discrete language diffusion is less mature than work on continuous image and video diffusion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the main questions is how to design the diffusion process for language. With images, there’s a very natural notion of adding a little bit of Gaussian noise. With text, because it’s discrete, there are many choices. You can mask tokens, you can replace tokens, you can work in a continuous representation. And it’s not clear yet which of those choices gives us the best way to learn the structure of language.

Another question is the tradeoff between parallel generation and the number of refinement steps. An autoregressive model generates one token at a time. A diffusion model can update many tokens simultaneously, but it may need to revisit them multiple times. So when does that actually give us an advantage in efficiency, and how much quality do we lose if we reduce the number of steps?

And then I think there’s a more fundamental question: what can we gain from being able to revise a whole sequence? In principle, that seems useful for satisfying global constraints or making different parts of an answer consistent with each other. But how do we turn that flexibility into a reliable advantage? Those are questions where I think there’s still a lot to understand.

r001.rationale: It identifies choosing how to define the text diffusion process—such as masking, replacing tokens, or using continuous representations—as unresolved.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that inference is decoupled from training.

r003.rationale: It does not mention numerical differential-equation solvers or their use to accelerate sampling.

r004.rationale: It discusses choices of diffusion process and refinement steps, but does not identify how to incorporate information throughout that process as an open question.

r005.rationale: It notes that text is discrete while image diffusion has a natural Gaussian-noise formulation, but does not say research on discrete language diffusion is less mature than continuous image and video diffusion research.
